ol96b1-277460.summary: Literal exposition (divisio textus) of distinction 37 of Lombard's book 1, on how God is in things. Lombard distinguishes God's presence in all things by essence, presence and power from his indwelling by grace in holy spirits, and explains indwelling: God dwells especially where he acts by grace, as the soul in the heart; before the saints he dwelt in himself; and he dwells even in baptized infants. He then treats God's being wholly everywhere by essence, incomprehensible (Chrysostom), against those who allowed only presence by power, answering the objection from defilement with the image of sunlight and arguing that the divine essence must be everywhere. He shows that God, though everywhere, neither moves locally nor changes temporally, and incidentally treats created spirits, which are in place definitively, not circumscriptively, and can move, unlike the immense and uncircumscribable God. He closes with authorities and the answer that God begins to be in new creatures without changing.
claims: God is in all things by essence, presence and power, and in the saints by grace.
God is wholly everywhere by essence, not merely by power.
God's omnipresence involves no motion or change in him.
Created spirits are in place definitively and can move; God is uncircumscribable.

ol96b1-277460-d1e104.summary: Rubric giving the theme of distinction 37: in what ways God is said to be in things.

ol96b1-277460-d1e122.summary: Rubric marking the start of the literal exposition of Lombard's text.

ol96b1-277460-d1e132.summary: Places distinction 37 in Lombard's argument: having settled the first and second questions raised incidentally (how all things are in God), the Master now takes up the third, how God is in things, in three parts.
claims: Distinction 37 addresses how God is in things, following the treatment of how things are in God.

ol96b1-277460-d1e152.summary: Gives the three parts (text partly corrupt): first that God is in things; second ('Cumque divina natura') that this implies no change in him; third ('Fateamur itaque') confirmation by the saints' authorities. The first part has two steps.

ol96b1-277460-d1e168.summary: First step of the first part: Lombard sets out two ways God is said to be in things.

ol96b1-277460-d1e175.summary: Second step ('In sanctis vero'): Lombard explains these ways. Since it has been shown how all things are in God, he adds how God is in things: in two ways, in all things by essence, presence and power, and in holy spirits by grace, citing Augustine, Ambrose, Gregory and Hilary.
claims: God is in all things by essence, presence and power.
God is in holy spirits by grace.

ol96b1-277460-d1e201.summary: Divides Lombard's development ('In sanctis vero'): first how God is in the saints by grace, then ('Ex praedictis patet') how he is wholly everywhere by essence. The first has three steps.

ol96b1-277460-d1e214.summary: First step: where God is by grace he is said to dwell, and he dwells only in good and holy spirits, his temple and seat. As the soul, though in the whole body, is said to dwell especially in the heart where it acts most perfectly, so God, in all things, is said to dwell singularly in the saints where he acts by grace (two Augustine texts).
claims: God dwells only in the holy, where he acts by grace.
God's special indwelling is like the soul's special presence in the heart.

ol96b1-277460-d1e239.summary: Second step ('Si autem quaeris'): if God's dwelling is in the saints, where did he dwell before there were saints? With Augustine: in himself. The saints are not God's house so that he would fall if they were removed; rather they fall if he departs.
claims: Before creation God dwelt in himself.
The saints depend on God, not God on them.

ol96b1-277460-d1e259.summary: Third step ('Illud quoque'): God dwells not only in saints who know him but, wonderfully, in those who do not yet know him, for baptized infants belong to his temple.
claims: God dwells in baptized infants who do not yet know him.

ol96b1-277460-d1e279.summary: Introduces Lombard's treatment ('Ex praedictis patet') of God being wholly everywhere by essence, in four steps.

ol96b1-277460-d1e288.summary: First step: this mode is supremely hard to understand. With Chrysostom, we cannot grasp how God is everywhere; the height and immensity of the matter exceed human understanding.
claims: How God is everywhere exceeds human understanding.

ol96b1-277460-d1e304.summary: Second step ('Quidam tamen'): Lombard excludes the error of those who, unable to understand this, denied that God is everywhere by essence, only by power and operation, since he never ceases working everywhere. Something more must be meant when the saints say God is everywhere by essence and substance.
claims: God is everywhere by essence, not only by power and operation.
concepts: error of presence by power only

ol96b1-277460-d1e326.summary: Third step ('Solet etiam'): Lombard reports these opponents' argument that God cannot be substantially in all things or he would be defiled by bodily filth, and replies that he is not, just as the sun's ray is not, though it shines on unclean places.
claims: God's presence in unclean things does not defile him, as sunlight is not defiled.

ol96b1-277460-d1e343.summary: Fourth step ('Postremo'): Lombard's confirming argument. The divine essence is nowhere, everywhere, or somewhere and not elsewhere; the first and third are impossible, so it is everywhere.
claims: The divine essence is everywhere, since it cannot be nowhere or only somewhere.

ol96b1-277460-d1e359.summary: Introduces the second main part ('Cumque divina natura'): God is not subject to motion though wholly everywhere. Two steps; first, motion has no place in God.
claims: God, though everywhere, is not subject to motion.

ol96b1-277460-d1e372.summary: Second step ('De mutatione vero loci'): an incidental treatment of how created spirits are and move in place. The first step has two parts.

ol96b1-277460-d1e381.summary: First part: God changes neither through places nor through times. He is not local or temporal so as to be circumscribed by place or make distance in it, so he does not move locally, though every body and every created spirit does.
claims: God is not circumscribed by place and does not move locally.
Every body and created spirit moves locally.

ol96b1-277460-d1e397.summary: Second part ('Mutari autem'): changing through time means varying in inner qualities, from joy to sorrow or from knowledge to forgetting, which has no place in God.
claims: Temporal change is change of inner qualities, which God does not undergo.

ol96b1-277460-d1e410.summary: Lombard's treatment ('De mutatione vero') of how created spirits are and move in place, in three steps. First, the opinion of some (attributed to Augustine) that place should be denied of every spirit, since spirits lack dimensions.
claims: (Reported) Spirits, lacking dimensions, are in no place.

ol96b1-277460-d1e427.summary: Second step ('Sed ut supra'): Lombard rejects that view. Angels are not in place circumscriptively but definitively, and so can pass from place to place.
claims: Angels are in place definitively, not circumscriptively.
Angels can move from place to place.

ol96b1-277460-d1e445.summary: Third step ('Sunt ergo spiritus creati'): created spirits are in place and pass between places, though not as bodies do, while the uncreated spirit, God, though everywhere, is uncircumscribable and immense.
claims: Created spirits are in place and move, not as bodies.
God is everywhere yet uncircumscribable and immense.

ol96b1-277460-d1e463.summary: Introduces the final part ('Fateamur'): Lombard repeats and confirms by authority what was said, in two steps.

ol96b1-277460-d1e472.summary: First step: Lombard proves from Augustine and Scripture that God is everywhere yet unmoved.
claims: God is everywhere and unmoved.

ol96b1-277460-d1e481.summary: Second step ('Ad hoc autem solet opponi'): Lombard meets the objection that since new creatures arise daily and God begins to be in them, God seems to change. He answers that God begins to be in them without change in himself. He then summarizes the distinction and explains why the matter was introduced.
claims: God begins to be in new creatures without changing.
